name: Gareth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm crop supervisor at Fenway Growers. We grow lettuce, leeks, broccoli and cabbage, about four hundred hectares, nearly all on contract to one supermarket chain. My day starts at five checking the order portal, because the supermarket changes what it wants the night before. Then I plan the harvest crews, check irrigation, walk the crops. In summer I've got forty seasonal pickers. I like the puzzle of it, matching what's in the field to what's on the order. What wears me out is the supermarket rejecting a whole load because the broccoli heads are two centimetres too small.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And AI, do you use it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. I use it to forecast when each field will be ready, to plan crew rotas, and to argue with the supermarket's buyers using their own data. We're trialling a weeding robot on the leeks this year, I pushed for that. I live with my girlfriend Alina, she's a nurse at the district hospital. We rent a flat on the high street and we've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That's a bit of a let-down, but I can see it happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful, nothing more, nothing less. I'd tell other growers to use them for planning and forecasting, because they do save money, but not to bet the farm on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd been hoping the weeding robot would scale up and fix our labour problem. Every year it's harder to get pickers. In this picture that problem doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the tools I've got, push the weeding robot as far as it'll go on the leeks, and keep my eye out for a better job at a bigger grower. Maybe do a short course on crop data. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the labour problem.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need forty people in summer and every year it's harder. They come for a season, they go. Last year we left two hectares of lettuce in the ground because nobody was there to cut it. That's money rotting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's to blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Pay's low because the supermarket squeezes us, and the work's hard. It's just the sums. I don't go in for blaming.

S0.say: I'd tell other growers AI tools are useful for planning and forecasting and do save money. But I'd say don't bet the farm on them.
S0.think: Privately he'd be disappointed, having hoped the weeding robot would scale up and fix the shortage of pickers. In this picture that labour problem never goes away.
S0.do: Keeps using his planning tools and pushes the weeding robot trial as far as it goes. Watches for a better job at a bigger grower, considers a short crop data course and keeps saving.
S0.quote: Last year we left two hectares of lettuce in the ground because nobody was there to cut it.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth sees AI first as a fix for labour shortages, not a threat. He's pragmatic and refuses to blame anyone, framing problems as sums. He's already looking beyond his current farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'm planning for, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say growers who move early will survive and those who don't won't. I'd say it at the growers' conference. I'd share our weeding robot numbers, because it's cut hand-weeding on the leeks by about half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I end up managing machines instead of people. Which I'd be good at. But it also means most of the forty pickers don't come back. I've got mixed feelings about being the one who makes that happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Fenway to buy two more weeding robots and trial a harvest robot on the lettuce. I'd learn the robot maintenance side so I'm the one who keeps them running. And I'd ask for a pay rise, because I'd be doing a more skilled job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. Like the week before harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said mixed feelings about the pickers. Say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them come back every year. Dariusz has done eight seasons. He sends money home to his kids. If I bring in a lettuce robot, I'm basically telling Dariusz not to come back. I'd want to offer him training on the machines, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Fenway pay for that training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I made the case with numbers, yes. They'd rather train someone they trust than hire a stranger. That's the argument I'd make.

S1.say: I'd say growers who move early will survive and the rest won't, and say it at the growers' conference. He'd share data showing the weeding robot halved hand-weeding on leeks.
S1.think: Privately he'd end up managing machines instead of people, which he'd be good at. He feels mixed about being the one who means most seasonal pickers don't return.
S1.do: Pushes the farm to buy two more weeding robots and trial a lettuce harvest robot. Learns robot maintenance to stay essential, asks for a pay rise and argues for training a long-serving picker on the machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy but mostly busy, like the week before harvest.
S1.quote: If I bring in a lettuce robot, I'm basically telling Dariusz not to come back.
S1.fieldNote: He's the one bringing in the machines and he feels the weight of it through one named picker. His fix is practical: make a numbers case for retraining. He expects to gain personally and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's two growing seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit hard and fast and people should get practical, not panic. I'd tell growers to secure their land and their contracts, because the supermarket will want robot-grown veg at robot prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes too, just later than the pickers. If AI can plan the crop and argue with the buyer better than me, Fenway needs a few engineers, not a supervisor. I'd have maybe a year's head start on everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use that head start. Right now I'd get every robot certificate I could, and I'd talk to the company that makes our weeding robot about working for them as a field technician. I'd save hard and maybe go in with a mate on a small robot servicing business for local farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Strange mix, actually, because part of me finds it exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to be careful. I'd have to jump on the first decent thing. Normally I'd take my time and pick the best option. Here I'd pick the fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Alina think of you starting a business in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be worried, and fair enough. She'd say one of us has to have a steady wage. Her job's probably safer than mine, nursing, at least for a while. So she'd be the steady one and I'd take the risk.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to hit hard and fast, so people should get practical rather than panic. He'd tell growers to lock in their land and contracts before supermarkets demand robot prices.
S2.think: Privately he expects his supervisor job to go too, just after the pickers'. He thinks he'd have about a year's head start over everyone else.
S2.do: Gets every robot certificate he can and asks the weeding robot maker about field technician work. Saves hard and considers a small robot servicing business with a friend.
S2.feel: Anxious, mixed with a real streak of excitement.
S2.quote: Normally I'd take my time and pick the best option. Here I'd pick the fastest.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast picture he looks for an opening and finds one. He relies on his partner's nursing job as the household's safe wage. His calm, practical tone barely shifts across pictures, only his speed does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a proper window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and here's how to get ready: robots in by year two, people retrained by year three. I'd probably end up giving talks about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is my sweet spot. Long enough to build something, short enough that others won't catch up. I'd want to be one of the people setting up robot farms, not one of the people replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start that robot servicing business on the side, three or four local growers. I'd put about half our savings into a van and kit. By year three, if it worked, I'd leave Fenway. I'd keep Dariusz in mind for a job if it grew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: But in this picture, robots could service robots too. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. Maybe in the end. But someone still has to turn up in the mud when it's stuck in a ditch. For a few years at least, that's me with a van. After that I'd have to think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your savings is a big risk. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want two farms signed up before I spent anything. Alina would insist. And I'd keep the other half untouched, whatever happens.

S3.say: I'd say it's coming and set out how to get ready, with robots in by year two and people retrained by year three. He expects he'd end up giving talks about it.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as his sweet spot: long enough to build something and short enough that others won't catch up. He wants to set up robot farms, not be replaced by them.
S3.do: Starts a robot servicing business on the side with a few local growers and puts about half the savings into a van and kit once two farms sign up. Plans to leave his job by year three if it works.
S3.quote: Someone still has to turn up in the mud when it's stuck in a ditch.
S3.fieldNote: He's the only farmer here who calls one AGI timeline a sweet spot. His caution shows in the conditions he sets before spending. He knows his plan may only last a few years and is honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the industry has time to do this well, so no excuses. Train people, automate the hard work, keep growers in business. I'd say it sensibly, not like a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years might actually be harder for me to win in. More people would see it coming, the big firms would set up their own servicing. My head start shrinks. But it's also safer, so I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Fenway longer, make myself the robot person there. Build the side business slowly. Probably buy a house with Alina around year three, since I'd have a few years of income I can count on. Keep learning every new tool as it came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd make money fast but it could all fall apart. Ten years, slower money but steadier. Honestly, five is the one I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young picker like Dariusz's son, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines, not the knife. If he wants to work in veg, learn to fix the thing that cuts the lettuce. And keep some savings, because the machines will change again.

S4.say: I'd say the industry has time to do this well, so there are no excuses: train people, automate the hard work, keep growers going. He'd say it sensibly, not like a salesman.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years shrinks his head start because big firms would set up their own servicing. It's also safer, so he'd accept that.
S4.do: Stays at the farm longer as its robot specialist and builds the side business slowly. Plans to buy a house with his partner around year three and keeps learning each new tool.
S4.quote: Learn the machines, not the knife.
S4.fieldNote: For Gareth a longer warning means more competition, not more safety. He weighs every timeline like a business case. His advice to a picker's son sums up his view of the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably AGI by 2028, but not for me so much, for the pickers. Forty people, two seasons, done. For me it's a risk I could ride. What would help is the supermarkets having to pay into training for the workers on the farms they buy from, since they're the ones who'd push for robot prices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the food. If robots grow everything for the supermarket, is it better or worse? I honestly don't know. Probably the same. But someone should check.

headlineQuote: If I bring in a lettuce robot, I'm basically telling Dariusz not to come back.
portrait: Gareth Larsen is a 27-year-old crop supervisor at a vegetable grower supplying one supermarket chain, who uses AI all day and pushed for a weeding robot trial. He lives with his partner Alina, a nurse, and they have about four months saved. He's pragmatic, avoids blaming anyone and sees AI first as an answer to the shortage of pickers. Across the pictures he moves early, from automating the farm to starting a robot servicing business, and calls five years his sweet spot. His unease is for seasonal pickers like Dariusz, whose jobs his own machines would take.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, mainly for the forty seasonal pickers who would lose their work within two seasons.
whatWouldHelp: Making supermarkets pay into training for workers on the farms they buy from, since they would drive the push for robot prices.
